title: Poisoning approach and drug overdoses
summary: Poisoning in the ICU: initial approach and toxidromes, decontamination and enhanced elimination (AACT/EXTRIP), paracetamol, cardiotoxic overdoses (TCA, CCB, beta-blocker, digoxin), toxic alcohols, and an antidote reference with Indian availability notes.

topics.title: Initial approach and toxidromes
topics.summary: Resuscitate first, recognise the toxidrome, run the standard poisoning screen, and use the poisons information centre.

definition.text: Most poisoned patients survive with good supportive care. The priority is airway, breathing, circulation, glucose and seizure control, then a focused toxicological assessment.

steps.title: ABCDE with glucose
steps.detail: Airway (aspiration risk with GCS ≤ 8 - but avoid reflex intubation in opioid toxicity if naloxone works), oxygen, IV access, capillary glucose, temperature.

steps.title: History from all sources
steps.detail: What, how much (mg/kg), when, route, co-ingestants (alcohol), intent, pill bottles, family members, prescriptions; ask about household pesticides and plants.

steps.title: Examine for a toxidrome
steps.detail: Pupils, skin (sweat/dry), temperature, HR, BP, RR, bowel sounds, mental status, clonus/rigidity.

steps.title: Standard investigations
steps.detail: 12-lead ECG (QRS, QTc, R in aVR), VBG/ABG with lactate, electrolytes, creatinine, LFT, paracetamol (all intentional overdoses) and salicylate levels, serum osmolality (osmolal gap), CK, pregnancy test.

steps.title: Specific measures
steps.detail: Decontamination if indicated, antidote if available, enhanced elimination if criteria met (see topics).

steps.title: Seizures and agitation
steps.detail: Benzodiazepines first line (lorazepam 4 mg or midazolam 10 mg IM); avoid phenytoin in toxic seizures.

steps.title: Psychiatric assessment
steps.detail: All deliberate self-harm needs psychiatric evaluation before discharge; document capacity.

doseCards.dose: 0.04-0.4 mg, repeat every 2-3 min to RR > 10
doseCards.workedExample: Apnoeic: 0.4 mg IV; partial response: 0.1 mg aliquots; infusion 2/3 of total effective dose per hour

tables.title: Toxidromes
rows: Hot, dry, flushed, mydriasis, delirium, urinary retention, tachycardia, reduced bowel sounds
TCA, antihistamines, datura (common in India), atropine
SLUDGE/DUMBELS, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations, weakness
Agitation, mydriasis, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
Coma with relatively normal vital signs
SSRIs, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue combinations

redFlags.text: QRS > 100 ms, seizures, hyperthermia > 40 °C, or refractory hypotension: high-risk poisoning - ICU and toxicology advice.

pitfalls.text: Missing paracetamol co-ingestion: check levels in all intentional overdoses.
Attributing coma to alcohol without checking glucose, head CT and other toxins.

pearls.text: Serotonin syndrome develops over hours with clonus; neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days with lead-pipe rigidity.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Toxidromes reflect receptor systems: muscarinic blockade (anticholinergic), acetylcholinesterase inhibition (cholinergic), catecholamine excess (sympathomimetic), mu-opioid agonism, and GABA-A potentiation (sedative-hypnotics).
consultantNotes.evidence: - Management is largely based on toxicology consensus statements and observational evidence; RCTs are few [IBCC].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Flumazenil in mixed overdoses (seizure risk); routine urine drug screens (low yield).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- In India, pesticides (organophosphates, aluminium phosphide, paraquat), rodenticides (yellow phosphorus), datura, oleander and drug overdoses are leading causes; see agrochemical and snakebite modules.
- National Poisons Information Centre (AIIMS New Delhi) and regional centres provide 24-h advice.
- Medicolegal: every poisoning is a medico-legal case in India - inform police (MLC), preserve samples (gastric aspirate, blood, urine) for forensic analysis.

topics.title: Decontamination and enhanced elimination
topics.summary: When to use activated charcoal, gastric lavage and whole bowel irrigation, and when to dialyse (EXTRIP).

definition.text: Decontamination reduces absorption (activated charcoal, whole bowel irrigation, rarely lavage); enhanced elimination increases clearance (MDAC, urinary alkalinisation, extracorporeal treatment).

steps.title: Single-dose activated charcoal
steps.detail: 50 g within 1 h of a potentially toxic ingestion of an adsorbable drug (consider up to 2-4 h for large or sustained-release ingestions) if the airway is protected.

steps.title: Gastric lavage
steps.detail: Not routine. Consider only within 60 min of a life-threatening ingestion with a protected airway and no effective alternative. Contraindicated for corrosives and hydrocarbons.

steps.title: Whole bowel irrigation
steps.detail: PEG-electrolyte 1.5-2 L/h by NG until rectal effluent is clear: iron, lithium, sustained-release CCB/beta-blockers, body packers.

steps.title: Multiple-dose charcoal
steps.detail: Life-threatening carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine or theophylline: 50 g then 25 g every 4 h if bowel sounds present.

steps.title: Urinary alkalinisation
steps.detail: Salicylate (and phenobarbital, chlorpropamide): bicarbonate to urine pH 7.5-8.0 with K replacement.

steps.title: Extracorporeal treatment (EXTRIP)
steps.detail: Small, water-soluble, low protein-binding, low Vd toxins: lithium, salicylate, toxic alcohols, metformin (lactic acidosis), valproate, theophylline, carbamazepine, barbiturates. Intermittent HD preferred; CRRT if unstable.

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 50 g in 200-300 mL water; NG if intubated

tables.title: EXTRIP haemodialysis indications (selected)
rows: Impaired kidney function and Li > 4.0 mEq/L, or decreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening arrhythmia
Level > 100 mg/dL (> 90 with impaired kidneys), altered mental status, new hypoxaemia, or pH ≤ 7.20 despite treatment
Coma, seizures, new visual loss, pH ≤ 7.15, persistent acidosis, anion gap > 24, or methanol > 70 mg/dL with fomepizole (> 60 with ethanol, > 50 without ADH blockade)
tables.caption: Summarised from EXTRIP workgroup statements; see full documents for 'suggested' indications.

redFlags.text: Salicylate poisoning with altered mental status or rising level: dialyse - and avoid intubation if possible (loss of respiratory compensation can be fatal); if intubated, match high minute ventilation.

pitfalls.text: Charcoal for alcohols, iron, lithium, acids, alkalis or hydrocarbons - they do not bind.
Routine gastric lavage in drowsy patients without airway protection: aspiration risk outweighs benefit.

pearls.text: Lithium: chronic toxicity with modest levels can be more dangerous neurologically than acute ingestion with higher levels.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Charcoal adsorbs drugs in the gut and, with repeated doses, creates 'gut dialysis' by back-diffusion from blood. Dialysability depends on molecular weight, protein binding, volume of distribution and endogenous clearance.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- AACT/EAPCCT position papers on charcoal, lavage, WBI and MDAC [Chyka 2005; Benson 2013; Thanacoody 2015; AACT 1999].
- EXTRIP systematic reviews and recommendations [Decker 2015; Juurlink 2015; Roberts 2015].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Charcoal beyond 1 h; lavage in Indian pesticide poisoning (common practice but weak evidence).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Gastric lavage is widely performed in Indian emergency departments for pesticide poisoning; ensure airway protection and avoid it in hydrocarbon (kerosene) and corrosive ingestions.
- Intermittent haemodialysis is the most widely available ECTR in Indian hospitals.

topics.title: Paracetamol poisoning
topics.summary: Risk-assess with the nomogram, give acetylcysteine by the two-bag regimen, extend for massive ingestion, and know when to refer for transplant.

definition.text: Toxicity is possible after ≥ 200 mg/kg or ≥ 10 g (whichever is less) in 24 h. For single acute ingestion with known time (4-24 h), plot the level on the nomogram (ANZ/US treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 h; UK uses 100 mg/L).

steps.title: Activated charcoal
steps.detail: Within 2 h of ingestion ≥ 10 g/200 mg/kg (within 4 h for massive ingestion ≥ 30 g or ≥ 500 mg/kg).

steps.title: Level at ≥ 4 h
steps.detail: Plot on nomogram; treat if above line. Unknown time, staggered ingestion, or presentation > 8 h after a toxic dose: start NAC immediately and check level and ALT.

steps.title: Acetylcysteine
steps.detail: Two-bag: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Do not wait for levels if > 8 h after ingestion.

steps.title: Massive ingestion
steps.detail: Level > 2 × nomogram line (> 300 mg/L at 4 h) or ≥ 30 g: double the second bag (200 mg/kg over 16 h); consider haemodialysis if level very high with coma and lactic acidosis.

steps.title: End of infusion
steps.detail: Check paracetamol and ALT: stop if paracetamol < 10-20 mg/L and ALT normal/falling; otherwise continue 100 mg/kg/16 h and repeat.

steps.title: Liver failure
steps.detail: INR rising, encephalopathy, acidosis: continue NAC, refer to liver unit, apply King's College criteria (see liver failure module).

doseCards.dose: 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
doseCards.dilution: Bag 1 in 500 mL 5% dextrose; bag 2 in 1,000 mL
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 14 g in 500 mL over 4 h (125 mL/h), then 7 g in 1,000 mL over 16 h (62.5 mL/h)
doseCards.verify: Weight cap and local regimen (2-bag vs 3-bag).

tables.title: Paracetamol risk assessment
rows: Level; NAC if above 150 mg/L line at 4 h (nomogram)
Charcoal if < 2 h; level at 4 h
NAC if ≥ 200 mg/kg or 10 g in 24 h, or level > 20 mg/L, or ALT raised
Charcoal up to 4 h; double second NAC bag; toxicology advice

redFlags.text: Early coma and lactic acidosis with a very high level (> 700-800 mg/L): mitochondrial toxicity - consider haemodialysis with NAC.

pitfalls.text: Using the nomogram for staggered or modified-release ingestions.
Stopping NAC at a fixed time despite rising ALT or detectable paracetamol.

pearls.text: NAC is almost completely protective if started within 8 h of ingestion.

nodes.text: Charcoal if < 2 h; level at 4 h
End: paracetamol < 20 mg/L and ALT normal?
Continue NAC; liver unit if INR rising

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: In overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation saturate; more paracetamol is oxidised by CYP2E1 to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and binds hepatocyte proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis. NAC replenishes glutathione.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- ANZ 2020 guideline: two-bag NAC, massive ingestion modifications [Chiew 2020].
- US/Canada 2023 consensus [Dart 2023].
- SNAP: 12-h modified regimen reduced vomiting and anaphylactoid reactions [Bateman 2014].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Treatment line (100 vs 150 mg/L); fomepizole as adjunct in massive ingestion.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Paracetamol overdose is less common in India than pesticide poisoning but is rising in urban areas; IV NAC is available (2 g/10 mL ampoules).
- Paracetamol levels may not be available 24 × 7 in smaller hospitals: start NAC empirically if a toxic dose is possible.

topics.title: Cardiotoxic overdoses: TCA, beta-blockers, CCB, digoxin
topics.summary: Sodium bicarbonate for sodium-channel blockade, calcium and high-dose insulin for CCB/beta-blocker shock, digoxin Fab, lipid and ECMO as rescue.

definition.text: Drugs causing shock and arrhythmia: sodium-channel blockers (TCA, flecainide, carbamazepine) widen QRS; CCBs (especially amlodipine, verapamil, diltiazem) and beta-blockers cause bradycardia, vasodilation and myocardial depression; digoxin causes arrhythmias and hyperkalaemia.

steps.title: TCA / sodium-channel blockade
steps.detail: QRS > 100 ms, R in aVR > 3 mm, arrhythmia or hypotension: sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg bolus, repeat to narrow QRS; keep pH 7.45-7.55; hyperventilate if intubated. Benzodiazepines for seizures.

steps.title: CCB poisoning (consensus 2017)
steps.detail: First line: IV calcium, high-dose insulin (with dextrose), vasopressors/inotropes (noradrenaline or adrenaline), atropine for symptomatic bradycardia. Decontaminate (WBI for sustained-release).

steps.title: Refractory CCB
steps.detail: Increase insulin up to 10 units/kg/h, pacing for bradycardia, lipid emulsion in peri-arrest, VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock in centres where available.

steps.title: Beta-blocker poisoning
steps.detail: Atropine, glucagon (bolus then infusion), high-dose insulin, adrenaline/noradrenaline; propranolol behaves like a sodium-channel blocker (bicarbonate for wide QRS).

steps.title: Digoxin
steps.detail: Fab for life-threatening arrhythmia, K > 6 mmol/L in acute toxicity, or end-organ hypoperfusion. Treat hyperkalaemia with insulin-dextrose; avoid electrical pacing if possible.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Continuous ECG, arterial line, glucose every 15-30 min on HIET, K hourly, echocardiography to distinguish vasoplegia from pump failure.

doseCards.dose: 1-2 mEq/kg bolus, repeat to QRS < 100 ms
10% chloride 10-20 mL (or gluconate 30-60 mL), repeat every 10-20 min
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 20 mL 10% CaCl2 over 5-10 min; infusion 14-28 mL/h

doseCards.dose: 1 units/kg bolus, then 1 units/kg/h up to 10 units/kg/h
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 70 units bolus; infusion 70 units/h = 7 mL/h; dextrose 35 g/h (e.g. 25% dextrose 140 mL/h via central line)

doseCards.dose: 5 mg bolus (repeat to 10 mg), then 3-5 mg/h
doseCards.verify: Stock is usually insufficient for infusions in India.

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 100 mL bolus, then 17.5 mL/min for 30-60 min

redFlags.text: Amlodipine overdose can cause delayed (12-24 h) severe vasoplegia and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; monitor in ICU for at least 24 h.

pitfalls.text: Stopping high-dose insulin because glucose falls: give more dextrose instead.
Class IA/IC antiarrhythmics or physostigmine in TCA toxicity.

pearls.text: Use echo: CCB shock with good contractility needs vasopressors; poor contractility needs insulin/inotropes.

nodes.text: Overdose with hypotension / brady / wide QRS

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Sodium-channel blockade slows phase 0 depolarisation (wide QRS); hypertonic sodium and alkalaemia overcome it. CCBs block L-type channels, causing vasodilation, bradycardia and insulin resistance (myocardium shifts to glucose); high-dose insulin improves myocardial carbohydrate uptake and contractility.
consultantNotes.evidence: - CCB poisoning expert consensus (2017) [St-Onge 2017]. HIET review [Engebretsen 2011]. Lipid emulsion recommendations [Gosselin 2016]. Digoxin Fab review [Chan 2014].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Lipid emulsion outside local anaesthetic toxicity; methylene blue for refractory vasoplegia.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Digoxin Fab and glucagon are rarely available in Indian hospitals; HIET with dextrose, calcium and vasopressors are the practical mainstays.
- Yellow oleander (Thevetia) seed poisoning causes digoxin-like toxicity in South India and Sri Lanka; Fab is effective but scarce, so supportive care, atropine and pacing are used.

topics.title: Methanol and other toxic alcohols
topics.summary: Suspect methanol in hooch clusters, use osmolal and anion gaps, block alcohol dehydrogenase (fomepizole or ethanol), give folinic acid, correct acidosis and dialyse early.

definition.text: Methanol (illicit liquor, solvents) and ethylene glycol (antifreeze) are metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to toxic acids (formic acid; glycolate/oxalate), causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis, blindness (methanol), AKI (ethylene glycol) and death.

steps.title: Suspect
steps.detail: Clusters after drinking illicit liquor, visual blurring ('snowfield'), abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing; may follow a latent period of 12-24 h.

steps.title: Investigate
steps.detail: ABG (HAGMA), anion gap, measured osmolality (osmolal gap > 10-20 suggests toxic alcohol early), ethanol level, methanol level if available, creatinine, lactate; CT head (putaminal necrosis).

steps.title: Block alcohol dehydrogenase
steps.detail: Fomepizole (preferred) or ethanol when methanol > 20 mg/dL, or strong history with osmolal gap > 10 or acidosis. Ethanol target blood level 100-150 mg/dL.

steps.title: Correct acidosis
steps.detail: Sodium bicarbonate to pH > 7.3 (reduces formate entry into CNS).

steps.title: Cofactors
steps.detail: Methanol: folinic acid 50 mg IV q4-6h. Ethylene glycol: thiamine 100 mg and pyridoxine 50 mg IV q6h.

steps.title: Haemodialysis (EXTRIP)
steps.detail: Coma, seizures, new visual deficit, pH ≤ 7.15, persistent acidosis, AG > 24, or high methanol level. Continue ADH blockade during and after HD (double ethanol dose or fomepizole q4h).

doseCards.dose: 15 mg/kg, then 10 mg/kg q12h × 4, then 15 mg/kg q12h
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg: 1,050 mg load in 100 mL NS over 30 min; then 700 mg q12h

doseCards.dose: Load ~800 mg/kg, maintain 80-130 mg/kg/h; target 100-150 mg/dL
doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg oral: 56 g ethanol ≈ 175 mL of 40% spirit (diluted) load; maintenance 5.6-9.1 g/h ≈ 18-29 mL/h of 40% (double during HD)
doseCards.verify: Measure ethanol levels every 2-4 h; pharmacy protocol.

redFlags.text: Visual symptoms, pH < 7.15 or coma after illicit liquor: dialyse urgently - prognosis depends on time to HD.

pitfalls.text: A normal osmolal gap does not exclude late toxic alcohol poisoning (parent alcohol already metabolised).
Forgetting to increase ethanol/fomepizole dosing during haemodialysis.

pearls.text: Calculated osmolality = 2 Na + glucose/18 + urea/6 (mg/dL); each 10 mg/dL ethanol adds about 2 mOsm/kg.

nodes.text: ABG, AG, osmolal gap, ethanol, methanol level
Methanol > 20 mg/dL or OG > 10 / acidosis with history?
Fomepizole or ethanol; bicarbonate; folinic acid
Coma, seizures, vision loss, pH ≤ 7.15, AG > 24?
Continue blockade until methanol < 20 mg/dL and pH normal

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, causing optic nerve and basal ganglia injury and lactic acidosis. Folate-dependent metabolism clears formate. ADH blockade stops formation of toxic metabolites; HD removes both parent alcohol and formate.
consultantNotes.evidence: - AACT methanol guideline 2002 [Barceloux 2002]. EXTRIP methanol recommendations 2015 [Roberts 2015].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Fomepizole vs ethanol cost-effectiveness in mass casualty settings; CRRT vs intermittent HD.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- India regularly experiences 'hooch tragedies' with dozens to hundreds of victims; prepare a mass-casualty plan (triage by pH, ventilators, HD slots).
- Fomepizole is rarely available; oral ethanol (pharmacy-diluted spirit via NG) and early HD are the practical options. Methanol levels are usually unavailable - use osmolal and anion gaps.

topics.title: Antidote quick reference
topics.summary: Antidote, indication and adult dose for the agents an Indian ICU should be able to access.

definition.text: Antidotes are few but time-critical. Each ICU should know which antidotes are stocked on site, in the hospital, and regionally.

steps.title: Know your stock
steps.detail: Keep an antidote list with location, quantity and alternative suppliers; review annually.

steps.title: Dose for the whole course
steps.detail: Many antidotes need large total quantities (e.g. glucagon, NAC, hydroxocobalamin); order more early.

steps.title: Hypoglycaemic agents
steps.detail: Sulfonylurea overdose: dextrose for immediate correction, then octreotide 50 mcg q6h to prevent recurrence; observe 24 h.

steps.title: Methaemoglobinaemia
steps.detail: Dapsone, nitrites, aniline dyes, local anaesthetics: methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg if MetHb > 20-30% or symptomatic (not in G6PD deficiency).

steps.title: Cyanide
steps.detail: Smoke inhalation with lactate > 8 mmol/L, coma, shock: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV; thiosulfate alternative.

steps.title: Isoniazid
steps.detail: Refractory seizures (common with TB drugs in India): pyridoxine 1 g per g ingested (5 g if unknown) plus benzodiazepines.

doseCards.dose: 1 g per g INH (5 g if unknown)

tables.title: Antidote table
rows: 0.04-0.4 mg IV titrated; infusion 2/3 effective dose/h
200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h
Fomepizole 15 mg/kg then 10 mg/kg q12h; ethanol to 100-150 mg/dL
CaCl2 10% 10-20 mL; insulin 1 units/kg bolus then 1-10 units/kg/h
0.2 mg IV increments; avoid in mixed overdose/seizure risk
1 g per g ingested (5 g empirical)

redFlags.text: Recurrent hypoglycaemia after sulfonylurea ingestion: may last > 24 h (especially glibenclamide and in renal failure).

pitfalls.text: Flumazenil in an unknown overdose: may precipitate seizures (TCA co-ingestion, benzodiazepine dependence).

pearls.text: In methylene blue-refractory methaemoglobinaemia think G6PD deficiency or sulfhaemoglobinaemia; consider exchange transfusion.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Antidotes act by receptor antagonism (naloxone, flumazenil, atropine), metabolic blockade (fomepizole), replacing depleted substrates (NAC, pyridoxine), binding the toxin (Fab, hydroxocobalamin), or bypassing the toxic effect (calcium, insulin, glucagon).
consultantNotes.evidence: - Mostly consensus- and case-series-based; see individual topic references [IBCC; St-Onge 2017; Chiew 2020].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Optimal stocking quantities in resource-limited settings.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Many antidotes (fomepizole, Fab, hydroxocobalamin, glucagon in quantity) are scarce in India; regional antidote banks and poison centres (AIIMS NPIC) can help locate stock.
- Pralidoxime and atropine are widely stocked because of high OP poisoning burden.

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.adultDose: 0.04-0.4 mg IV, repeat every 2-3 min to adequate breathing (up to 10 mg); infusion two-thirds of the effective reversal dose per hour.
drugs.cautions: Precipitated withdrawal and pulmonary oedema with large doses; shorter half-life than many opioids.

drugs.name: Activated charcoal
drugs.indications: Recent ingestion (usually < 1-2 h) of a toxic amount of an adsorbable drug, airway protected
drugs.adultDose: Single dose 50 g (1 g/kg) orally/NG. Multiple-dose (carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline): 50 g, then 25 g every 4 h (or 12.5 g/h).
drugs.cautions: Aspiration; contraindicated with unprotected airway, ileus/obstruction, corrosives, hydrocarbons. Does not bind alcohols, metals (iron, lithium), acids/alkalis.

drugs.name: N-acetylcysteine
drugs.indications: Paracetamol poisoning above nomogram line or with liver injury
drugs.adultDose: Two-bag regimen (ANZ): 200 mg/kg over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Traditional 3-bag: 150 mg/kg over 1 h, 50 mg/kg over 4 h, 100 mg/kg over 16 h. Continue 100 mg/kg/16 h until criteria met.
drugs.preparationIndia: 200 mg/mL; Indian 2 g/10 mL ampoules; dilute in 5% dextrose or NS.
drugs.cautions: Anaphylactoid reactions (fewer with 2-bag/12-h regimens): pause, antihistamine, restart slower.
drugs.verify: Weight cap (ANZ: actual weight up to 110 kg) and doubled second bag for massive ingestion.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4%
drugs.indications: TCA/sodium-channel blocker cardiotoxicity (QRS > 100 ms); salicylate; methanol acidosis
drugs.adultDose: Sodium-channel blockade: 1-2 mEq/kg (mmol/kg) IV bolus, repeat to QRS narrowing, target pH 7.45-7.55. Salicylate: 1-2 mEq/kg bolus then infusion to urine pH 7.5-8.
drugs.preparationIndia: 8.4% = 1 mEq/mL; 7.5% (0.9 mEq/mL) in many Indian hospitals.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride 10% / gluconate 10%
drugs.adultDose: CCB: calcium chloride 10% 10-20 mL (or gluconate 10% 30-60 mL) IV, repeat every 10-20 min or infusion (chloride 0.2-0.4 mL/kg/h); target ionised Ca up to 2× normal.

drugs.name: Insulin (high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy)
drugs.indications: CCB and beta-blocker poisoning with myocardial dysfunction
drugs.adultDose: 1 units/kg IV bolus, then 1 units/kg/h, titrate every 10-15 min up to 10 units/kg/h; dextrose 25 g bolus if glucose < 250 mg/dL, then 0.5 g/kg/h; glucose every 15-30 min, potassium hourly.
drugs.preparationIndia: Concentrated infusion e.g. 500 units in 50 mL NS (10 units/mL) to limit volume.
drugs.cautions: Hypoglycaemia (may persist for hours after stopping), hypokalaemia.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.adultDose: 3-10 mg (0.05-0.15 mg/kg) IV over 2-5 min, then 3-5 mg/h infusion.
drugs.cautions: Vomiting (protect airway), hyperglycaemia; expensive and often unavailable in large quantities in India.

drugs.name: Lipid emulsion 20%
drugs.indications: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity; refractory lipophilic drug cardiotoxicity (bupivacaine, some CCB, TCA) as rescue
drugs.adultDose: 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 1 min, then 0.25 mL/kg/min (repeat bolus once or twice; max ~10-12 mL/kg).
drugs.cautions: Interferes with lab tests, pancreatitis, ARDS; recommended for LAST; only rescue for other drugs.

drugs.name: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab)
drugs.indications: Digoxin toxicity with life-threatening arrhythmia, K > 6 mmol/L, end-organ dysfunction
drugs.adultDose: Acute: 2-5 vials (40 mg each) titrated; empirical 10 vials for cardiac arrest. Chronic: 1-2 vials.

drugs.name: Fomepizole
drugs.adultDose: 15 mg/kg IV over 30 min, then 10 mg/kg q12h × 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h; q4h during haemodialysis.

drugs.name: Ethanol (antidote)
drugs.adultDose: Load 600-800 mg/kg (IV 10% ethanol ~8 mL/kg, or oral 40% spirit ~2 mL/kg diluted); maintenance 80-130 mg/kg/h (higher in drinkers and doubled on haemodialysis); target blood ethanol 100-150 mg/dL.
drugs.cautions: CNS depression, hypoglycaemia, phlebitis; needs ethanol levels every 2-4 h.
drugs.verify: Pharmacy-prepared IV ethanol or oral spirit protocol; volumes depend on concentration.

drugs.name: Folinic acid (or folic acid)
drugs.adultDose: Folinic acid 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg) IV q4-6h (folic acid 50 mg IV q6h if unavailable).

drugs.name: Octreotide
drugs.adultDose: 50 mcg SC/IV every 6 h (or 25-50 mcg/h infusion).

drugs.name: Methylene blue
drugs.adultDose: 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 min; repeat after 1 h if needed.
drugs.cautions: Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.

drugs.name: Hydroxocobalamin
drugs.adultDose: 5 g IV over 15 min (repeat 5 g if needed).
drugs.verify: Availability in India limited; sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate alternative.

drugs.name: Pyridoxine
drugs.adultDose: 1 g per g of isoniazid ingested (unknown: 5 g IV over 5-15 min).
drugs.verify: High-dose IV pyridoxine availability in India.
